summary: Describes the security mechanisms for IPv4 and IPv6 and the services they provide. It is the original overall architecture for IPsec as a standards-track document, later replaced by RFC 2401.

plainLanguage.summary: This document lays out how security is added to IP. It defines two extra headers, one that proves a packet was not altered and one that also hides its contents, and it explains the table of keys and algorithms that both of them need. It is the original architecture of what later became IPsec.

questions: what is the ip security architecture
how does ip authentication header work
what is the difference between ah and esp
subtitle: The overall design for securing IP: two headers, a set of security associations, and rules for managing keys.

tldr.problem: The Internet protocol offers no protection of its own: a packet's contents can be read, altered or forged by anyone on the path.
tldr.mechanism: The architecture defines two mechanisms. The Authentication Header computes a cryptographic value over the datagram, and the Encapsulating Security Payload encrypts it. Both need a Security Association, identified by a Security Parameters Index and a destination address, which holds the algorithms and keys.
tldr.outcome: The RFC sets out what each mechanism provides, how the two can be combined, and what key management an implementation must support. It was later replaced by RFC 2401.

facts.label: Security Association identifier
facts.value: The SPI value together with the Destination Address

facts.label: Traffic analysis protection
facts.value: Not provided by any of these mechanisms

facts.value: Manual configuration of Security Associations MUST be supported

today: RFC 1825 was a Proposed Standard published in August 1995. It has been obsoleted by RFC 2401, which is the current security architecture for the Internet Protocol.

sections.title: What IP-Layer Security Covers
sections.content:
The memo describes the security mechanisms for IP version 4 and IP version 6 and the services they provide. Each security mechanism is specified in a separate document. It also describes key management requirements for systems implementing those mechanisms. It is not an overall security architecture for the Internet and is instead focused on IP-layer security.

The document starts with a set of definitions. Authentication is the property of knowing that the data received is the same as the data that was sent and that the claimed sender is in fact the actual sender. Integrity is the property of ensuring that data is transmitted from source to destination without undetected alteration. Confidentiality is the property of communicating such that the intended recipients know what was being sent but unintended parties cannot determine what was sent, and encryption is a mechanism commonly used to provide it. Non-repudiation is the property of a receiver being able to prove that the sender of some data did in fact send it, even though the sender might later want to deny it. Traffic analysis is the analysis of network traffic flow for the purpose of deducing information useful to an adversary, such as frequency of transmission, the identities of the conversing parties, packet sizes and the Flow Identifiers used.

Two specific headers provide the security services in IPv4 and IPv6: the IP Authentication Header and the IP Encapsulating Security Payload header. The Authentication Header is designed to provide integrity and authentication without confidentiality, and the lack of confidentiality is deliberate: it keeps implementations of the Authentication Header widely available, even where the export, import or use of encryption is regulated. It supports security between two or more hosts implementing AH, between two or more gateways implementing AH, and between a host or gateway implementing AH and a set of hosts or gateways.

A security gateway is a system which acts as the communications gateway between external untrusted systems and trusted hosts on their own subnetwork, and it provides security services for those trusted hosts when they talk to the external systems. A trusted subnetwork contains hosts and routers that trust each other not to engage in active or passive attacks and trust that the underlying communications channel is not being attacked. Where a security gateway provides services on behalf of hosts on a trusted subnet, the gateway establishes the security association on behalf of its trusted host, so only the gateway needs to implement AH or ESP while the systems behind it can still benefit.
sections.plainLanguage: Security at the IP layer means four things: proving who sent a packet, proving it was not altered, hiding its contents, and being able to prove later that it was really sent. This document covers the first three at the IP layer and says nothing about hiding the fact that traffic is flowing at all.

sections.title: Security Associations
sections.content:
The concept of a Security Association is fundamental to both the Encapsulating Security Payload and the Authentication Header. The combination of a given Security Parameters Index and a Destination Address uniquely identifies a particular Security Association, and an implementation of either mechanism MUST support this concept. A Security Association normally includes the authentication algorithm and algorithm mode and the keys used with it for AH, and the encryption algorithm, mode and transform and the keys used with it for ESP. It also holds the presence, absence and size of any cryptographic synchronisation or initialisation vector field, the lifetime of the key or the time when a key change should occur, the lifetime of the Security Association itself, the source addresses of the Security Association, which might be a wildcard address if more than one sending system shares the same Security Association with the destination, and the sensitivity level of the protected data.

The sending host uses the sending userid and the Destination Address to select an appropriate Security Association and hence an SPI value, while the receiving host uses the combination of SPI value and Destination Address to distinguish the correct association. When a formerly valid Security Association becomes invalid, the destination systems SHOULD NOT immediately reuse that SPI value, and instead SHOULD let it become stale before reusing it for some other Security Association.

A security association is normally one-way, so an authenticated session between two hosts normally has two Security Parameter Indexes in use, one in each direction. The receiver-orientation of the Security Association implies that in the case of unicast traffic the destination system will normally select the SPI value, so there is no potential for manually configured Security Associations that conflict with automatically configured ones. For multicast traffic there are multiple destination systems but a single destination multicast group, so some system or person must select SPIs on behalf of that group and communicate the information to the legitimate members by mechanisms not defined in the document. Multiple senders to a multicast group MAY use a single Security Association, in which case the receiver only knows the message came from a system knowing the security association data for that group and cannot generally authenticate which system sent it when symmetric algorithms are in use.
sections.plainLanguage: A Security Association is one row of a table: it says which algorithm to use, which key, and how long it lasts. The receiver finds the right row using the number in the packet plus the destination address, and the table is normally one-way, so each direction of a conversation has its own row.

sections.title: The Two Mechanisms
sections.content:
There are two cryptographic security mechanisms for IP. The first is the Authentication Header, which provides integrity and authentication without confidentiality. The second is the Encapsulating Security Payload, which always provides confidentiality and, depending on the algorithm and mode, might also provide integrity and authentication. The two may be used together or separately.

The Authentication Header holds authentication information for its IP datagram. It does this by computing a cryptographic authentication function over the datagram and using a secret authentication key in the computation. The sender computes the authentication data before sending the authenticated packet, and the receiver verifies its correctness on reception. Fields that must change in transit, such as the IPv4 TTL or the IPv6 Hop Limit, are omitted from the authentication calculation. The default authentication algorithm is keyed MD5, which, like all symmetric algorithms, cannot provide non-repudiation by itself. Confidentiality and traffic analysis protection are not provided. All IPv6-capable hosts MUST implement the Authentication Header with at least the MD5 algorithm using a 128-bit key, and IPv4 systems claiming to implement it MUST do the same.

The Encapsulating Security Payload is designed to provide integrity, authentication and confidentiality. It does this by encapsulating either an entire IP datagram or only the upper-layer protocol data inside the ESP, encrypting most of the ESP contents, and then appending a new cleartext IP header to the now encrypted payload. That cleartext header is used to carry the protected data through the internetwork.

There are two modes within ESP. Tunnel mode encapsulates an entire IP datagram within the ESP header. Transport mode encapsulates an upper-layer protocol, for example UDP or TCP, inside ESP and then prepends a cleartext IP header. When both hosts directly implement ESP and there is no intervening security gateway, they may use Transport mode, where only the upper layer protocol data is encrypted and there is no encrypted IP header. That mode reduces both the bandwidth consumed and the protocol processing costs for users who do not need to keep the entire IP datagram confidential. For interoperability throughout the worldwide Internet, all conforming implementations of ESP MUST support the Data Encryption Standard in Cipher-Block Chaining mode.

In some cases the Authentication Header might be combined with the Encapsulating Security Payload. The Authentication Header always provides integrity and authentication and can provide non-repudiation if used with certain algorithms such as RSA. The Encapsulating Security Payload always provides integrity and confidentiality and can also provide authentication if used with certain authenticating encryption algorithms. When the two are combined, the placement of the Authentication Header makes clear which part of the data is being authenticated.
sections.plainLanguage: The Authentication Header checks that a packet is genuine and unaltered but leaves the contents readable. The Encapsulating Security Payload hides the contents as well, either the whole packet or just the data inside it.

sections.title: Key Management
sections.content:
The key management protocol to be used with IP layer security is not specified in this document. Because the key management protocol is coupled to AH and ESP only via the Security Parameters Index, the RFC can meaningfully define AH and ESP without fully specifying how key management is performed. Several key management systems are envisioned as usable, including manual key configuration.

Support for key management methods where the key management data is carried within the IP layer is not a design objective. Instead these mechanisms will primarily use key management methods where the key management data is carried by an upper layer protocol such as UDP or TCP on some specific port number, or where it is distributed manually. This permits a new key management method to be substituted without modifying the implementations of the other security mechanisms.

Manual key management, where a person configures each system with its own key and with the keys of other communicating systems, is quite practical in small, static environments but does not scale. The RFC reviews other approaches: Needham and Schroeder proposed a key management algorithm relying on a centralised key distribution system, used in the Kerberos Authentication System developed at MIT under Project Athena, and Diffie and Hellman devised an algorithm that does not require a centralised key distribution system, although the original technique is vulnerable to an active man in the middle attack, a vulnerability that can be mitigated by using signed keys to authentically bootstrap into the Diffie-Hellman exchange.

There are two keying approaches for IP. Host-oriented keying means all users on one host share the same key for traffic destined for all users on another host. User-oriented keying gives one user on one host one or more unique session keys for traffic destined for another host, not shared with other users. When host-oriented keying is used and mutually suspicious users exist, user A can sometimes determine the host-oriented key by well known methods such as a Chosen Plaintext attack, and then read or forge user B's traffic. Support for user-oriented keying SHOULD be present in all IP implementations.

All implementations covered by the requirements MUST support manual configuration of Security Associations, SHOULD support an Internet standard Security Association establishment protocol once one is published as an Internet standards-track RFC, and MAY support other methods. Given two endpoints it MUST be possible to have more than one concurrent Security Association. An IP system MUST take reasonable steps to protect the keys and other security association information from unauthorised examination or modification, because all of the security lies in the keys.
sections.plainLanguage: The headers do not say how keys reach the two ends. That is a separate protocol, and the document only fixes the one thing the two must agree on: the number that names the security association in the packet.

sections.title: Where These Mechanisms Are Used
sections.content:
The document describes possible uses in several environments. With firewalls, both mechanisms can increase the security a firewall provides. A firewall used with IP often needs to parse the headers and options to determine the transport protocol and the port number in use. A firewall that is not party to the applicable Security Association will not normally be able to decrypt an encrypted upper-layer protocol to view the protocol or port number needed to perform per-packet filtering, so authentication might be performed not only within an organisation or campus but also end to end with remote systems across the Internet.

With IP multicast, the SPIs used in the IP security mechanisms are receiver-oriented, which makes them well suited to multicast, though most currently published multicast key distribution protocols do not scale well. As an interim step a multicast group could repeatedly use a secure unicast key distribution protocol to distribute the key to all members, or the group could pre-arrange keys using manual key distribution.

For quality of service protection, the Authentication Header might be used to provide authentication of packets, which is potentially important in packet classification within routers. The IPv6 Flow Identifier might act as a Low-Level Identifier, and used together packet classification within routers becomes straightforward if the router is provided with the appropriate keying material. For performance reasons the routers might authenticate only every Nth packet rather than every packet.

In compartmented or multi-level networks, where a single network carries data at different sensitivity levels, the mechanisms are designed to support strong mandatory access controls. If explicit IP sensitivity labels are used and confidentiality is not needed in the operational environment, the Authentication Header is used to provide authentication for the entire packet, including cryptographic binding of the sensitivity level to the IP header and user data. IPv6 will normally use implicit sensitivity labels that are part of the Security Association but not transmitted with each packet. All explicit IP sensitivity labels MUST be authenticated using either ESP, AH, or both.
sections.plainLanguage: The document works through four situations: a firewall that needs to know what is inside a packet, a multicast group, a router that wants to prioritise packets by who sent them, and a network that carries several levels of classified material at once.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC is explicit that this is a security architecture for the Internet Protocol and not a general security architecture for the Internet. Cryptographic transforms for ESP which use a block-chaining algorithm and lack a strong integrity mechanism are vulnerable to a cut-and-paste attack and should not be used unless the Authentication Header is always present with packets using that ESP transform.

If more than one sender shares a Security Association with a destination, the receiving system can only authenticate that the packet was sent from one of those systems and cannot authenticate which of them sent it. Similarly, if the receiving system does not check that the Security Association used for a packet is valid for the claimed Source Address, it cannot authenticate whether the claimed Source Address is valid: if senders A and B each have their own unique Security Association with destination D, and B uses its valid Security Association with D but forges a Source Address of A, then D will be fooled into believing the packet came from A unless D verifies that the claimed Source Address is party to the Security Association that was used.

The quality of the security provided depends completely on the strength of the implemented cryptographic algorithms, the strength of the key being used, the correct implementation of those algorithms, the security of the key management protocol, and the correct implementation of IP and the security mechanisms in all participating systems. The security of the implementation is in part related to the security of the operating system that embodies it: if the operating system does not keep the private cryptologic keys confidential, then traffic using those keys will not be secure. Because different users on the same system might not trust each other, each user or each session should usually be keyed separately.

Certain security properties, such as traffic analysis protection, are not provided by any of these mechanisms, and one possible approach is appropriate use of link encryption. Certain applications, such as electronic mail, probably need application-specific security mechanisms, which are out of the scope of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: The security you get is only as good as the algorithm, the key, the key management and the implementation. If several senders share one security association, the receiver cannot tell which of them sent a packet, and if it does not check that the claimed source address matches the association, it can be fooled.

items.title: Security Parameters Index
items.text: A 32-bit number that, with the destination address, names the association.

items.title: Algorithms and modes
items.text: The authentication algorithm for AH; the encryption algorithm, mode and transform for ESP.

items.title: Keys
items.text: The keys used with those algorithms.

items.title: Initialisation vector
items.text: Its presence, absence and size, for the encryption algorithm.

items.title: Lifetimes
items.text: When the key changes, and when the association itself expires.

items.title: Source addresses
items.text: Which senders may use it, possibly a wildcard address.

items.title: Sensitivity level
items.text: The level of the protected data, for example Secret or Unclassified.

viz.caption: THE KEY MANAGEMENT APPROACHES THE RFC CONSIDERS

items.title: Manual configuration
items.text: A person configures each system with its own key and its partners' keys. Practical in small static environments, but it does not scale.

items.title: Centralised distribution
items.text: Needham and Schroeder's algorithm, used in the Kerberos Authentication System.

items.title: Diffie-Hellman
items.text: No centralised distribution needed, but the original technique is vulnerable to an active man in the middle attack.

items.title: Signed bootstrap
items.text: Signed keys used to authenticate into the Diffie-Hellman exchange, which mitigates that attack.

items.title: Automated distribution
items.text: An Internet-standard, scalable Security Association establishment protocol, still to be specified at the time of writing.
